newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. force in Macedonia renewed but size cut.
newsitem.headline: U.N. force in Macedonia renewed but size cut.

text.p: The Security Council on Wednesday approved a six-month renewal, until May 31, 1997, of a 1,100-member U.N. force stationed in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia but ordered a phased 300-man reduction in its strength.
The vote was 14 to none, with Russia abstaining.
Speaking before the vote, Russian U.N. envoy Sergei Lavrov said the current renewal should be the last one. But because this was not spelled out in the resolution, he could not support it.
The resolution called for the force's military component to be cut by 300 soldiers by April 30, 1997, "with a view to concluding the mandate as and when circumstances permit."

Known formally as the U.N. Preventive Deployment Force (UNPREDEP), it currently includes some 500 U.S. troops, 500 from the Nordic countries, a 50-member Indonesian heavy engineering platoon, 35 military observers and a number of civilian police monitors.

It was sent to Macedonia in late 1992 to deter any spread of violence from other parts of the former Yugoslavia, then embroiled in conflict, and was the first U.N. force dispatched as a purely preventive operation.

A recent report by Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said it had become "increasingly evident that the primary threat to the country's stability may come from internal political tensions." He was alluding to ethnic divisions involving the country's large Albanian minority.

"UNPREDEP has accordingly devoted considerable attention to strengthening dialogue between the political forces and has assisted in monitoring human rights and inter-ethnic relations," the secretary-general said.

The timing of the force reduction would allow for this "to be fully effected after the severe winter conditions have passed and for the (U.N.) secretariat to undertake the necessary consultations with troop-contributing countries," he added.
